title: ASUS builds humanoid robot to pack tiny parts in electronics factories
content: Taiwanese technology company ASUS is developing a humanoid robot called Gallop to automate repetitive tasks in electronics manufacturing. The robot’s customer pilot programs are planned for 2027, and commercial availability is targeted for the second half of 2028.The robot is currently being tested at an ASUS group electronics manufacturing services (EMS) factory, where it is learning to pack motherboard accessories at a workstation designed for human workers.According to ASUS, Gallop is being developed to show that humanoid robots can consistently perform real factory operations rather than simply complete staged demonstrations.Humanoid learns factoryGallop’s initial assignment involves packing 15 different motherboard accessories, many of which are small, thin, and enclosed in transparent plastic bags. The task presents a challenge for conventional robotic grippers because of the different shapes and flexible materials involved.ASUS said it selected the workstation to test whether Gallop could take responsibility for most of an operation without requiring a human worker to remain alongside it throughout the process.Meet Gallop at work. Its first job: packing motherboard accessories, 15 small parts, many in soft bags. It learns by watching our own workers, then practicing on the same parts. Albert Chang explains how:https://t.co/8gtKPDuey4 #ASUS #AI #PhysicalAI pic.twitter.com/CF3iCBmblh— S.Y. Hsu (@SYHsuASUS) November 13, 2026The company has developed a training process that combines human demonstrations, simulation, and hands-on practice. With their consent, experienced factory workers wear small head-mounted cameras to record how they perform specific operations. Gallop uses this information to learn the movements and handling techniques required for the job. Simulation software then generates variations of the demonstrations to help the robot handle minor differences in working conditions.The training process also includes virtual reality (VR), with an operator wearing a headset and gloves to guide Gallop through tasks using the same components and cameras found at the actual workstation. Once deployed, the robot’s recorded experiences will also feed back into its training process.The company has set a target of achieving 99.5 percent task success within 20 seconds, matching the time required for a human worker to complete the same operation.Gallop gets smarterASUS has divided Gallop’s AI architecture into four layers: planning, supervision, skills, and control. The planning layer interprets the surrounding environment and breaks an operation into individual steps. A separate supervisory AI monitors these actions and can revise the plan when something goes wrong. The skills layer manages movements such as reaching, grasping, and placing objects, while the control layer operates the robot’s arms and hands.The architecture uses fixed interfaces between the different layers, allowing ASUS to replace AI models as improved versions become available without redesigning the entire robot. The system runs on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor computer installed inside Gallop, alongside standard robotics software.ASUS is developing the robot’s body and dexterous hands in-house. The hands are particularly important because they need to manipulate small components while using tactile sensing to understand physical contact. Other components, including motors, are sourced from established industry partners.Gallop currently operates from a fixed base equipped with two arms. ASUS plans to introduce a wheeled version and integrate its in-house dexterous hand over the coming year. The company also intends to demonstrate the robot to customers at Computex 2027, ahead of planned pilot deployments.Electronics manufacturing will be its first target market, although ASUS sees potential applications in hospitals and other service environments. The company believes that skills learned at one workstation could be transferred to other operations involving similar pick-and-place activities.ASUS said Gallop is intended to handle repetitive and physically demanding tasks rather than replace factory workers. Employees involved in training the robot could instead move into roles involving robot setup, supervision, and performance improvements.The Gallop program began in early 2026. ASUS is targeting customer pilots in 2027 and market availability in the second half of 2028. However, the robot’s ability to meet its factory performance targets remains an important part of its development.

title: Elon Musk's SpaceX and Tesla move closer to historic merger deal
content: SpaceX could announce a deal to acquire Tesla as early as December after talks between Elon Musk’s two companies advanced to negotiations over price and control, Bloomberg reported on November 12.A combination would be the world’s largest merger, according to the report. SpaceX is valued at more than $1.9 trillion following its June initial public offering, while Tesla is worth about $1.5 trillion.The boards and advisers of both companies are involved in the talks, which could continue into early 2027. One question is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive if the rocket maker absorbs the electric vehicle company. Neither company commented, and Tesla shares rose as much as 1.9% after the report.Negotiators turn to deal termsMusk raised the possibility of combining Tesla and SpaceX in May, weeks before SpaceX went public. In October, he confirmed that both boards had formed special committees to explore a merger.Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees, has also served on SpaceX’s board since February.The talks come ahead of Tesla’s December 3 annual shareholder meeting. Investors will vote on whether to reelect Musk, board chair Robyn Denholm, and director JB Straubel to terms running through 2029. The ballot also includes votes on executive compensation and the company’s auditor.The companies’ current valuations put their combined market value at roughly $3.4 trillion. For comparison, Vodafone’s takeover of Mannesmann in 2000 was valued at $183 billion. SpaceX bought Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI for roughly $250 billion earlier this year.A share swap would change voting rightsMusk owns about 20 percent of Tesla. At SpaceX, he controlled roughly 85 percent of the voting power through shares carrying extra votes, according to the company’s IPO filing. Tesla investors who receive SpaceX stock would move from a company where each share carries one vote to one where Musk holds a commanding majority of the votes.A deal could also accelerate Musk’s compensation. Under the change-of-control terms of his 2025 CEO award, operating milestones would fall away, and the deal price would determine whether Tesla meets the market value thresholds. A deal valuing Tesla at $2 trillion would clear the first threshold, triggering immediate vesting for the shares earned at that level. That implies a 33 percent premium over Tesla’s current valuation. His 286 million in restricted shares from a 2018 award would also vest early.Tesla’s China operations pose a hurdleHow to keep Tesla’s China business separate is among the main issues facing negotiators, Bloomberg reported.A JPMorgan analyst described SpaceX’s government and defense work and Tesla’s presence in China as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” for regulators and shareholders.Tesla’s Shanghai factory makes more than half of its cars and shipped 67,829 vehicles in October. In July, The Wall Street Journal reported that Tesla was considering a sale or spinoff of its China operations. Musk denied the report.Bloomberg previously reported that the companies wanted to close the deal before President Donald Trump leaves office. Democrats took control of Congress in the midterms and have said they would scrutinize Musk’s companies and political ties.

title: NYC bans businesses from using personal data to set different prices

content: New York City has approved legislation targeting businesses that use personal information to determine how much individual customers pay. The measure prohibits companies from using algorithms and consumer data to charge different prices for identical goods and services.The City Council approved Introduction 891-A on November 12. Sponsored by Council Speaker Julie Menin, the legislation targets surveillance pricing, a practice that can make the same product cost different amounts depending on the customer. The measure ranks among the strongest restrictions on surveillance pricing in the country.How surveillance pricing worksSurveillance pricing relies on algorithms that analyze personal information when determining what customers pay. Businesses can potentially use shopping behavior, location data, and other personal details to adjust prices for individual consumers. These systems can operate behind the scenes, leaving shoppers unaware that their personal information influences the prices they see.Some companies use your personal data, like browsing history, to serve different prices to different costumers. It’s called surveillance pricing, and we just banned it in New York City.This tweet will say the same thing in incognito mode, don’t worry.— Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani (@NYCMayor) November 13, 2026Several investigations have uncovered examples of this practice across different industries. One investigation found that a major grocery delivery platform conducted algorithmic pricing experiments. Those tests produced price differences of up to 23 percent for certain products.Another investigation documented a television price increase at a retail store. The television reportedly cost $499.99 before its price climbed to $599.99 when the shopper entered the store’s parking lot.Ride-hailing services have also faced scrutiny over personalized pricing. A behavioral economist who previously worked for a major ride-share company revealed how low phone battery levels could influence fares.The application reportedly increased prices when a customer’s battery ran low. Its pricing system potentially exploited situations where customers had fewer alternatives for getting home.Businesses face new restrictionsIntroduction 891-A defines surveillance pricing as a pricing method determined entirely or partially by algorithms using personal data. The practice involves offering different prices to customers purchasing identical goods or services.Menin described the Council’s approval as an important consumer protection measure against businesses exploiting personal information.“When corporations use algorithms and personal data to charge different people different prices for the same products, it’s unethical and worsens our affordability crisis,” Menin said.The legislation gives the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection authority to investigate complaints and issue fines of up to $1,000 per violation.Each affected consumer or transaction can constitute a separate violation. That provision could increase financial penalties for businesses applying individualized pricing across large customer groups.Small businesses also receive an opportunity to correct certain violations promptly and avoid penalties. The legislation preserves legitimate promotional offers, including loyalty rewards, student discounts, and veteran discounts.Buy-one-get-one-free promotions also remain permissible under the restrictions. These exemptions distinguish ordinary promotional pricing from algorithms that use personal information to determine individualized prices.The Council’s approval establishes a new restriction on how businesses can use consumer data when setting prices in New York City. It also gives local regulators an enforcement mechanism against surveillance pricing practices across the five boroughs.

title: Chip-based lasers cool trapped ions 3x faster for quantum computing
content: Researchers at Cornell University have developed a chip-based laser-cooling technique that brings trapped ions close to their quantum ground state in just 150 microseconds, potentially reducing a major time bottleneck in quantum computing.The method is around three times faster than a conventional laser arrangement, which takes approximately 500 microseconds. It also cools three different modes of an ion’s motion simultaneously, rather than requiring separate cooling operations for each mode.The findings demonstrate how integrated photonics could improve the control of trapped ions as researchers work to build larger quantum computers.The study was led by Karan Mehta, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at Cornell’s Duffield College of Engineering. Cooling slows quantum operationsTrapped-ion quantum computers use electrically charged atoms held in electromagnetic fields to store and process quantum information. Their precision makes them promising candidates for quantum computing, but unwanted atomic motion can interfere with operations.Researchers must repeatedly use lasers to remove this motion and cool ions close to their lowest possible energy state. These cooling procedures can take up a substantial portion of a quantum computer’s operating time.Mehta said cooling, particularly to the quantum ground state, has become a major bottleneck in leading trapped-ion systems.To address this, the Cornell team developed an approach that delivers carefully controlled laser light through integrated optical components on a microfabricated ion-trap chip.The researchers directed two laser beams in opposite directions to create a standing wave, a pattern of alternating high- and low-intensity regions. They positioned a trapped calcium ion at a low-intensity point, or node, to suppress unwanted light interactions that can heat the ion while cooling its motion.Standing waves accelerate coolingThe team combined this optical arrangement with a technique called electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) cooling. It brought the targeted motion close to the quantum ground state in about 150 microseconds, compared with roughly 500 microseconds using a conventional running-wave laser setup.The experiment also demonstrated simultaneous cooling across three measured motional modes spanning approximately 5 megahertz. The targeted mode reached an average phonon occupancy of around 0.05, while the researchers brought the measured modes close to their ground states.The results also demonstrated cooling below the conventional Doppler limit, experimentally verifying a long-standing theoretical prediction.An important part of the approach is its integrated optical delivery system. The chip routes multiple wavelengths, from ultraviolet to near-infrared light, needed to control the ion. The team also developed packaging that allowed the device to operate at cryogenic temperatures.The chips were commercially fabricated in the Netherlands through a collaboration with ETH Zurich, while Cornell facilities helped prepare the devices for the experiments. Scaling trapped-ion computersThe demonstration involved a single calcium ion, rather than a multi-ion quantum processor. However, the researchers said the approach could be applied to larger trapped-ion systems.Integrating optical components into ion-trap devices could reduce the need for complex external laser arrangements as processors scale to more qubits. Faster cooling across multiple motional modes could also reduce the time spent preparing ions for quantum operations.The researchers said the work shows how technologies being developed to scale quantum computers could also improve the fundamental operations that those systems rely on.The study was published in PRX Quantum.

title: Mars robot swarms get new GPS-free navigation tech for exploration
content: Researchers in Germany are developing a navigation system that could help autonomous robot swarms explore Mars without relying on satellite-based positioning. The technology will combine star and Sun sensors with a network of radio beacons, allowing robots to determine their location and direction across the Red Planet’s difficult terrain.The work is part of VaMEx-ARES, a new three-year research project involving the University of Würzburg. The German Space Agency at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) has awarded around $1.54 million to two research teams at the university for the work, which began in October 2026.The project forms part of the wider VaMEx initiative, which aims to explore Valles Marineris, a vast canyon system stretching approximately 1864 miles across Mars. Its proposed robotic swarm would include flying, walking and wheeled machines working together to investigate the region, including caves that may exist beneath its surface. Robots navigate without GPSUnlike Earth, Mars does not have a network of navigation satellites that robots can use to establish their positions. This makes autonomous exploration particularly challenging, especially when machines need to operate across uneven terrain and coordinate with one another.Guido Dietl, a professor of satellite communication and radar systems at the University of Würzburg, is leading work on a navigation system to address this problem.His team plans to combine measurements from star and Sun sensors with positioning data collected through a network of radio beacons. The system will use ultra-wideband (UWB) technology to measure distances and angles to the beacons.By combining these measurements, the robots should be able to calculate their positions and travel directions independently. Researchers intend to integrate the navigation hardware and software into the swarm gradually and validate the systems through future field tests under Mars-like conditions. Cameras help coordinate robotsA second focus of the research is the development of SkyCAM, a camera system created by the team of Hakan Kayal, a professor of space technology at the university.The system is designed to automatically detect short-lived phenomena in the sky, including lightning, cloud formations, and meteors. Researchers are now adapting it for integration onto the Janus Mars rover.The team also plans to test SkyCAM during the Austrian Space Forum’s AMADEE-27 analog mission in Portugal, scheduled for April 5–18, 2027. The campaign will simulate conditions on Mars to help researchers assess equipment before potential use in space exploration.Researchers hope to deploy two or three SkyCAM stations during the tests. By recording the same moving objects from different locations and synchronizing their data, the cameras could help estimate an object’s distance, speed and flight path.That information could also support navigation across the robot swarm, allowing its different machines to share observations and coordinate their movements. Preparing for Mars explorationVaMEx has been running since 2012 and has now entered its fourth development phase. The latest work builds on previous research, with teams now developing the hardware, software and system architecture needed to coordinate different types of robots.The wider VaMEx-ARES consortium includes researchers from the University of Bremen, the German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, the Technical University of Braunschweig, the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg and RWTH Aachen University.The technologies are not yet ready for a Mars deployment. Researchers will first integrate the navigation and sensor systems into the robotic swarm and test them through analog missions and field trials.If successful, the work could help future missions explore areas that are difficult for conventional rovers to reach, including deep valleys and underground environments.

title: Spacecraft refueling port costs just $1 ahead of historic orbital test
content: Spacecraft could soon share a common refueling connection, potentially changing how operators manage satellites in orbit. Spaceium has released OpenPort, an open-source interface that any company can license and manufacture for just $1.The design lets spacecraft receive fuel after launch instead of relying entirely on their onboard reserves. It will also undergo an orbital demonstration aboard the International Space Station.Common refueling standardMost satellites carry a fixed supply of propellant for their planned missions. Once that supply runs low, operators often retire otherwise functional spacecraft. Their electronics and other systems might remain operational, but limited fuel can end their usefulness.A lack of standardized connections has also complicated orbital refueling efforts. Different manufacturers develop their own interfaces, forcing operators to consider compatibility before arranging fuel transfers. A tanker built by one company might not connect with another manufacturer’s spacecraft.OpenPort aims to address that problem through an identical connection on both spacecraft. Its androgynous design allows either vehicle to supply or receive propellant. That means a satellite could potentially refuel another spacecraft instead of relying exclusively on dedicated tankers.The interface also replaces a conventional fill-and-drain valve. Those connections typically serve ground fueling operations before launch. OpenPort keeps the connection functional after a spacecraft reaches orbit.Spaceium says its design handles higher pressures and greater docking misalignment than competing refueling interfaces. These capabilities could help spacecraft establish reliable connections during demanding orbital operations.Xenon transfer reaches orbitOpenPort’s upcoming demonstration will take place aboard the International Space Station. Spaceium plans to fly the hardware as a NASA-approved external payload through Voyager Technologies’ commercial payload service.During the demonstration, the interface will transfer xenon between two tanks in orbit. Spaceium describes this as the first-ever xenon transfer performed in orbit. The mission will test whether spacecraft can exchange propellant through a standardized connection.The demonstration follows another Spaceium mission in February 2026. Its precision robotic actuator successfully completed its first space mission after launching aboard a SpaceX rideshare.Building a refueling networkSpaceium wants OpenPort to become a widely adopted connection across the spacecraft industry. Its broader business model centers on automated orbital stations that sell propellant as a service.Co-founder and CEO Ashi Dissanayake says the company sees the stations as its primary business. Every spacecraft equipped with OpenPort could eventually become a potential customer.“The port isn’t the business. The stations are,” Dissanayake said. He believes widespread adoption will create demand for orbital refueling services, including those operated by competitors.Founded by aerospace and mechanical engineers Dissanayake and Reza Fetanat, Spaceium joined Y Combinator’s Summer 2024 batch. Its commercial customers include operators pursuing orbital transfer vehicles, lunar missions and geostationary satellites.The company plans to establish refueling stations across low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit. Its longer-term ambitions also include stations along routes to the Moon.A common connection could eventually help satellite operators extend spacecraft lifespans. It could also allow lunar missions and orbital transfer vehicles to travel farther without carrying all their propellant from Earth.Spaceium is expanding its engineering team as it prepares for the ISS demonstration and its first refueling station. OpenPort’s adoption will ultimately determine whether different spacecraft manufacturers embrace a shared standard.

title: SpaceX's 6-gigawatt campus will use dry cooling, skip groundwater use
content: SpaceX plans to invest around $50 billion in a supercomputing campus in Arizona, using a dry-cooling system designed to reduce the facility’s reliance on water. The project is part of a wider expansion worth more than $74 billion across Arizona and Texas as the company scales up its computing infrastructure.The proposed campus in Cochise County would use air-based cooling instead of conventional water-intensive systems. SpaceX also said it does not plan to use industrial groundwater for the facility, an important distinction for a project planned in an arid region where water availability is a major concern.Dry cooling limits water useThe Arizona facility is expected to create around 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent positions, according to SpaceX. The company is also working with local electric cooperatives to supply electricity to the campus.SpaceX said the development could reduce electricity bills for cooperative members by up to 20 percent. The project would require significant power infrastructure, with its plans outlining a campus of nine computing buildings and capacity of up to 6 gigawatts when fully developed. However, the development is not yet approved. SpaceX needs permission from Cochise County, where the proposal has drawn opposition from some residents. A petition with around 2,400 signatures has asked county officials to reject the project, with a public hearing scheduled for December. Texas brings water investmentThe Arizona campus is one part of SpaceX’s planned expansion. The company has also announced an investment of more than $24 billion in a supercomputing facility at its Starbase site in Texas.Unlike the Arizona project, the Texas facility is expected to generate its own electricity rather than draw power from the public grid. A separate public filing describes a proposed 750-megawatt natural gas-fired power plant alongside the computing campus. The gas plant remains a proposal and should not be confused with SpaceX’s announcement of the supercomputing facility. The Texas development has also brought a major water infrastructure commitment for nearby Brownsville. SpaceX has pledged up to $220 million for water and wastewater projects in the city and Cameron County, with $40 million provided initially under the agreement.The company said the investment would support projects capable of adding 20 million gallons of water capacity per day. However, Brownsville’s approved plans identify two projects expected to add approximately 18 million gallons daily: an 8-million-gallon-per-day potable water reuse system and a 10-million-gallon-per-day expansion of the Southmost Regional Water Authority facility. The agreement does not give SpaceX ownership of the water infrastructure or reserved capacity in the system. The projects are intended to strengthen the region’s water supply as Brownsville and surrounding communities continue to grow.Together, the two campuses represent a major expansion of SpaceX’s computing ambitions, with the Arizona project highlighting an approach to reducing industrial water demand and the Texas development combining dedicated power generation with a substantial regional water investment.

title: 930 mph supersonic aircraft gets advanced military mission systems
content: American defense startup Hermeus is joining forces with Northrop Grumman to develop advanced mission capabilities for next-generation unmanned military aircraft. The partnership aims to combine high-speed flight technology with sophisticated onboard systems for future U.S. military operations.The agreement brings Northrop Grumman into Hermeus’ aircraft development efforts. The defense contractor will help design, develop, integrate, and maintain mission systems for Hermeus’ reusable, high-Mach aircraft. These platforms aim to give American forces faster and more affordable options for demanding missions.Hermeus wants to develop aircraft that can operate at speeds beyond conventional military platforms. Its recent supersonic flight milestone offers an indication of how quickly the startup is advancing its aircraft development program.Integrating advanced mission systemsNorthrop Grumman will contribute technologies that help unmanned aircraft perform more complex military tasks. Its work will cover sensing, communications, navigation, and command-and-control capabilities. These systems will help aircraft process mission information and coordinate operations.The collaboration also combines two different engineering approaches. Northrop Grumman brings decades of experience developing mission equipment for military aircraft. Hermeus contributes a faster development process and an internally developed mission management system.Hermeus’ mission management system uses an open, modular architecture. It separates flight-critical functions from mission-critical operations. This distinction allows engineers to update mission capabilities without disrupting essential aircraft controls.The architecture follows several U.S. government standards. These include the Agile Mission Suite and Autonomy Government Reference Architectures. It also supports Open Mission Systems and the Universal Command and Control Interface.Such compatibility could make future upgrades considerably easier. Hermeus says its architecture can help engineers integrate new capabilities within weeks instead of years. That flexibility matters as military requirements change and new technologies become available.Hermeus CEO Zach Shore said Northrop Grumman’s experience would help expand what its aircraft can accomplish. He also pointed to the potential for faster deployment of operational capabilities.Supersonic testing gains momentumHermeus has already demonstrated progress with its Quarterhorse aircraft program. Its Quarterhorse Mk 2.1 recently completed its first supersonic flight, reaching Mach 1.21. The aircraft achieved that speed during its third test flight over White Sands Missile Range airspace.The milestone arrived less than three months after the aircraft’s maiden flight. It also came 364 days after the first flight of Hermeus’ earlier Mk 1 demonstrator.Quarterhorse Mk 2.1 represents the first of three F-16-sized supersonic aircraft in Hermeus’ development roadmap. It uses the Pratt & Whitney F100 engine, which comes from RTX’s Pratt & Whitney business.Hermeus follows an iterative development strategy. Engineers build successive aircraft and use flight-test data to refine their designs. Each prototype helps the company evaluate performance and address technical risks before advancing further.Work on the next aircraft has already begun. Quarterhorse Mk 2.2 is undergoing development and testing, with Mk 2.3 expected to follow.Each aircraft will push the program toward sustained high-Mach flight. The Northrop Grumman partnership could also help bring increasingly sophisticated mission equipment into that development process.Both companies intend to pursue advanced defense programs that need high-performance aircraft and established mission technologies. Their combined expertise could help the U.S. military explore new unmanned aviation capabilities without waiting for traditional aircraft development cycles.

title: Microsoft outage affects 130,000 users as server failures spread
content: Microsoft is still working to restore services after a widespread outage disrupted access to Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft 365 applications. The disruption affected nearly 130,000 users globally, according to reports collected by Downdetector. Microsoft now believes unavailable servers and problems with automated health checks contributed to the incident.The software giant has started bringing affected infrastructure back online. However, some users continued experiencing connectivity problems as recovery efforts progressed Thursday.Server failures caused disruptionMicrosoft traced the disruption to an infrastructure problem that left several servers unexpectedly unavailable. Those failures increased the workload on remaining servers, creating additional pressure across its infrastructure.The company said overall traffic had not increased enough to explain the elevated load. Instead, unavailable servers forced the remaining infrastructure to handle more requests than usual.We're actively restarting and validating the affected servers to return them to service. In parallel, we're assessing whether reverting a small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the…— Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026An issue with automated server health checks may have contributed to the problem. These checks help Microsoft determine whether individual servers are functioning correctly. However, a failure in that process apparently prevented some servers from remaining available.The resulting connectivity problems affected several Microsoft 365 products. Users reported difficulties accessing Outlook mailboxes and sending or receiving emails. Others struggled to load Teams and Microsoft’s productivity applications.Downdetector recorded nearly 130,000 reports during the outage’s peak. Reports covered Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint and OneDrive. Microsoft’s Copilot assistant also experienced disruptions.Microsoft tests recovery measuresMicrosoft has begun validating an alternative health-check method to bring affected servers back online. The approach has already worked on a subset of impacted machines.The company is now expanding that fix across its affected infrastructure. It is also developing an automated process to identify unresponsive servers and restart them.Microsoft previously said it was restarting affected machines to restore availability. The company also paused deployments and configuration changes while investigating potential causes.Its investigation identified recent configuration updates as a possible contributor. Microsoft is now assessing whether reversing some of those changes could speed up recovery.In its latest update, Microsoft said it was actively restarting and validating affected servers. It also confirmed that engineers were evaluating whether reverting selected configuration updates would accelerate the process.The company has not confirmed that configuration changes directly caused the outage. Its investigation remains ongoing.Recovery remains underwayMicrosoft previously reported progress in restoring Teams services across North America. However, reports from affected users indicated that connectivity problems had not disappeared entirely.The disruption also exposed how failures within individual infrastructure components can affect several interconnected services. Microsoft’s cloud-based applications depend on extensive server infrastructure to handle authentication, communications, and data access.Automated health checks play an important role in maintaining that infrastructure. They help operators identify malfunctioning machines before those failures affect wider services. A problem with the checks themselves can complicate that process.Microsoft’s recovery efforts now involve restoring unavailable servers and examining recent infrastructure changes. The company has yet to provide a definitive explanation for the underlying failure.Users experiencing continued problems may still encounter intermittent access issues as Microsoft works through its recovery process.

title: SpaceX proposes 750 MW gas plant for Texas supercomputing hub
content: SpaceX is seeking approval to set up a 750-megawatt (MW) natural gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility at Starbase,Texas.The company separately confirmed on Thursday plans to invest more than $24 billion in the supercomputing project, which will generate its own electricity without drawing power from the public grid.The proposed facilities are part of a broader development plan for which SpaceX has sought a property tax abatement and a related economic development agreement, according to a public hearing notice issued by the City of Starbase. The city commission is scheduled to consider both requests at a public hearing on December 9.Multi-billion project​To develop the said facilities, the company has proposed an investment of $24 billion, which would be the largest private technology investment ever proposed in the Rio Grande Valley as the company seeks to expand its artificial intelligence computing capabilities.​The company said the proposed project would be built on roughly 444 acres near the Port of Brownsville and would combine a natural gas power plant with a large-scale data center designed to support AI workloads.The project has already generated more than 3,000 construction jobs and is expected to support more than 500 permanent positions once operational. The planned investment builds on more than $15 billion the company has already invested in Starship and related infrastructure at Starbase.​It would construct, own, and operate both the power plant and the supercomputing campus. The space company has been focusing on producing electricity from fossil fuels to power Musk’s larger ambitions in the AI space. Building its own power generation facility could allow SpaceX to avoid lengthy waits for grid connections, an increasingly common challenge for developers of large AI data centers.According to SpaceX, the supercomputing facility will train frontier intelligence systems for applications spanning medical research, emergency response, advanced manufacturing and national security. It will also help develop and test technologies for future space-based computing.​The proposal also aligns with Elon Musk’s broader AI ambitions. SpaceX has rapidly expanded beyond its traditional launch business by investing heavily in computing infrastructure that supports AI services. The company has reported strong growth in AI-related revenue while renting computing capacity to customers including Google and Anthropic.The company also announced a $220 million project to expand Brownsville’s water and wastewater infrastructure. The company described this as the largest private contribution to the city’s water future in its history and said it has already provided $40 million to the Brownsville Public Utilities Board to begin the work.The proposed water projects could add approximately 20 million gallons per day of additional capacity through potable water reuse and expanded brackish-groundwater treatment. The investment is intended to strengthen regional water security and reduce dependence on the Rio Grande.SpaceX’s other natural gas projects ​In October, SpaceX sought approval for a 32.4-mile natural gas pipeline in Florida to supply fuel for its Starship rockets as the company prepares to expand launch operations at Cape Canaveral.The proposed 16-inch transmission pipeline would run through Brevard County and connect SpaceX facilities with the existing Florida Gas Transmission interstate pipeline, and bring natural gas directly from the interstate network to customers including SpaceX.Florida is not SpaceX’s first attempt to build a dedicated natural gas connection for Starship. The company has also sought approval for an approximately 8-mile pipeline serving its Starbase launch complex near Boca Chica in South Texas.The two projects point to a broader effort to establish dedicated fuel infrastructure around SpaceX’s major Starship launch sites. The Florida pipeline would be about four times as long as the proposed Texas connection.Once approved, the Starbase project would rank among the largest private investments in South Texas and further transform the company’s launch site into a hub for both space exploration and AI infrastructure. The December 9 hearing will determine whether SpaceX receives the requested tax incentives needed to move the project forward.

title: Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen for faster coding and agentic tasks
content: Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen, adding another model to its frontier lineup alongside Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon within a matter of days.Built for rapid execution across agentic workflows, Hydrogen brings Google’s latest model capabilities to everyday coding, software development and other tasks that require speed and efficiency.Unlike Carbon and Argon, which are designed for deep, long-horizon reasoning on complex problems, Hydrogen focuses on fast execution. It can write code, run tests, verify changes, and handle routine development tasks, either independently or alongside the other Gemini 4 models.Hydrogen also surpassed Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, scoring 51 against Argon’s 50 at the default high thinking level. Its score rises to 54 at the highest xhigh setting, according to Google.Faster coding and smarter executionGoogle designed Hydrogen to handle everyday developer workloads, including debugging, repository coding, web development and multi-step agentic tasks. It can also process text, images, audio, and video, with a combined input-output context window of up to 1 million tokens.The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high, and a new xhigh setting, allowing developers to adjust reasoning depth according to a task’s complexity, latency, and cost requirements.In Google’s evaluations, Hydrogen scored 57 percent on Terminal-Bench 4.1, more than three times the 18.2 percent recorded by Gemini 3.8 Flash. The company also says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than its predecessor at the default high setting.For broader knowledge work, the model can analyze documents, spreadsheets, charts, and recorded video to produce reports and structured outputs. Google also highlights improvements in tool use, coding accuracy, and its ability to recover when a tool call fails or a search returns no results.Orchestrating multiple modelsGoogle is also introducing Orchestrator in its Antigravity development platform, allowing developers to combine Gemini 4 Carbon and Hydrogen within a single session.Rather than relying on one model throughout a task, Orchestrator dynamically switches between the two based on the work required. Carbon can initially examine a codebase, resolve ambiguities, and create an execution plan, while Hydrogen takes over routine coding, package updates, and testing. If the faster model encounters difficulties, the task can return to Carbon for further reasoning and adjustments.On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator achieved task success rates close to Carbon while consuming 24 percent less usage quota and completing tasks 19 percent faster on average, Google said.The approach is intended to reduce the need to use a high-reasoning model for every step of a development workflow, potentially lowering costs while maintaining performance.Google is rolling out Hydrogen across Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, and Google Search. It is also available to paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Antigravity, while Orchestrator is initially rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers.The model’s API pricing is set at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens across its 1-million-token context window.

title: Smart drone could find risky hidden cracks in old concrete bridges
content: A smart autonomous drone invented by researchers in Germany could reportedly make bridge inspections faster, safer and significantly cheaper by uncovering tiny, hidden cracks in the concrete. The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) was made by David Müller, MSc, and Raphael Dyrska, PhD, both research associates at Ruhr University Bochum, and their team. According to the scientists, the autonomous system can explore narrow, poorly lit areas inside bridge structures and scan concrete surfaces for damage. It uses AI to find hairline cracks that human inspectors might otherwise miss, and can even plan its own flight routes, while storing inspection data directly on a SD card. Its aim is to reduce the workload of bridge inspectors as aging infrastructure faces increasing pressure from traffic and environmental conditions.The system is currently undergoing lab tests. The team hopes to demonstrate its capabilities inside a real bridge. “Our drone can make inspections safer, faster, and more affordable,” Müller elaborated. Smarter bridge inspectionsThousands of bridges in Germany require annual inspections, as many were built between the 1960s and 1980s and were not designed to withstand today’s traffic volumes. Heat, frost and other environmental factors can severely damage their concrete surfaces. Even though detecting cracks as early as possible is crucial to keeping them safe, conventional inspections can be both time-consuming and prone to human error. “Inspectors normally work on site with a clipboard and a camera. This approach is demanding and prone to error,” Patrick Herbers, MSc, a research assistant at the university, and one of the experts involved in the project, said. However, Herbers pointed out that their drone could address these challenges by accessing areas that are difficult or potentially dangerous for human inspectors to reach. Its compact size allows it to fly inside narrow, hollow sections of concrete bridges, where it scans the surrounding walls for cracks.At the same time, the device uses simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), a technology that enables autonomous machines to determine their position and map unfamiliar environments simultaneously. It can therefore find its way without external positioning systems. The next challengeThe drone is currently being tested at the flight laboratory run by Ruhr University Bochum’s Chair of Control Engineering and Systems Theory. The facility is located at the Center for the Engineering of Smart Product-Service Systems (ZESS).The team now plans to test the technology inside a real bridge to see how well it performs in real-life conditions. “We want to demonstrate that our drone not only works in laboratory settings, but also in practice,” Marcel Neuhausen, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher at the Ruhr University Bochum’s Artificial Intelligence and Formal Methods Department, said. Despite potential concerns, the researchers insist that the drone will not replace human inspectors. It will rather collect inspection data and flag critical areas, and leave the final assessment of structural damage to qualified professionals.The research team believes this could speed up the digitalization of infrastructure inspections and address the growing shortage of bridge inspectors. “The number of bridge inspectors is decreasing, the demands are growing, and the bridges aren’t getting any younger,” Müller concluded in a press release.

title: 100% hydrogen turbines could power AI data centers with lower emissions
content: GE Vernova unveiled two major hydrogen-ready milestones for its aeroderivative gas turbines at COP31 in Antalya. Both milestones emerged from a newly inaugurated hydrogen testing laboratory at the company’s Global Technology Center in Greenville, South Carolina.“These milestones represent a crucial step in GE Vernova’s commitment to accelerating the energy transition by providing hydrogen-ready solutions that allow customers to lower carbon emissions while maintaining the rapid-start reliability essential for grid stabilization,” said Cecilia Giovannelli, CEO of GE Vernova’s Gas Power Aeroderivative gas turbine business.Hydrogen testing facility at the Global Technology Center in Greenville, South Carolina. Image credit: GE VernovaFast-starting turbinesThe current surging power demand from hyperscale AI data centers has created an urgent need for aeroderivative turbines. These units give operators quick, on-site power that avoids long grid delays and meets clean energy goals.First, the Cambridge-based firm announced the validation of the modular LM2500XPRESS gas turbine package to run on fuel blends containing up to 50 percent hydrogen in a Dry Low Emission (DLE) configuration. Interestingly, the unit keeps its signature speed. Operators can still bring the turbine to full power in five minutes or less, giving utilities and data centers an immediate safety net when renewable energy dips or demand spikes.“With more than 1150 units sold and more than 200 million operating hours, the LM2500 remains one of the world’s most widely adopted gas turbines, supporting mission-critical applications ranging from industrial cogeneration and district heating to data centers and grid support,” the company noted. Second, GE Vernova tested its LM6000VELOX platform to run on 100% hydrogen. Although it was not straightforward. Achieving stable combustion with pure hydrogen presents severe hurdles, as the gas burns hotter and faster than natural gas. Those risks were mitigated with an advanced Single Annular Combustor (SAC) system. It proved the turbine can operate entirely without carbon-based fuels and showed reliable operation across a global footprint of nearly 1,350 units.New testing infrastructureThe new Greenville laboratory sits at the center of this momentum. Announced as part of a broader U.S. manufacturing investment in 2025, the dedicated facility conducts tests under real conditions and cut down development lead times for customers worldwide.These latest tests build on an extensive operational track record. Across more than 120 gas turbines worldwide, GE Vernova has logged over 11 million operating hours using hydrogen and hydrogen-blended fuels. The firm has already demonstrated its hydrogen blend technology at key commercial sites across multiple continents. Real-world deployments and tests are underway at DeBary in Florida and NYPA Brentwood in New York, as well as at Australia’s Tallawarra B Power Station and China’s Guangdong Huizhou facility.Steelmakers, refiners, and grid operators can now transition to clean energy without immediately replacing their existing power plants. Modular upgrades and retrofits let facilities burn current fuel blends right away and steadily prepare for a 100% hydrogen future.Validating the turbines in Greenville proves the engines can handle the fuel, but wide commercial rollout still hinges on green hydrogen supply, pipeline infrastructure, on-site storage, and competitive fuel costs. Existing LM2500 and LM6000 operators also cannot simply pump hydrogen into unmodified machines, as reaching 50 percent or 100 percent blends requires dedicated hardware, fuel-skid, and control-system upgrades.

title: China discovers major natural gas reservoir 18,930 feet under Bohai Sea
content: Reports suggest China has tapped into a massive volcanic reservoir that could help power millions of homes across the capital region.China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) announced the discovery of a “high-yield volcanic oil and gas well” in deep formations of the central Bohai Sea. Reportedly, the reservoir lies 5,770 meters (18,930 feet) down in this region. The find sits adjacent to the Bozhong Sag, the largest hydrocarbon-rich depression in the Bohai Sea. The discovery could support China’s push to extract natural gas from extreme offshore environments.Volcanic gas well in Bohai SeaDuring testing, the well yielded about 800,000 cubic meters of natural gas per day from a cumulative gas-pay zone more than 120 meters thick in volcanic rock. For the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region and the broader Bohai Rim, this area serves as a vital energy lifeline.“The success of this well has opened up a new play for offshore ultra-deep natural gas exploration ​and expanded the ​scope ⁠of deep oil and gas exploration in Bohai,” said Xu Changgui, ​chief scientist and chief geologist of ​CNOOC, as Reuters reported.However, drilling at such depths comes with a lot of challenges. Extreme heat flow, intense tectonic activity, and complex rock structures make it difficult to predict underground reservoirs. To overcome these obstacles, CNOOC independently developed multi-source broadband three-dimensional seismic technologies, along with new methods for identifying high-quality reservoirs in ultra-deep buried hills.Gas-bearing pay zones in volcanic formations are underground layers of cooled magma and ash that hold commercially extractable natural gas. In sedimentary reservoirs, gas rests between sand grains, whereas in volcanic rock traps, gas is trapped inside tiny eruption-formed bubbles and tectonic fractures. Over millions of years, natural gas migrates upward from deeper source rocks into these porous pockets, where a dense overlying rock layer seals it in place.Beijing’s energy security goalsThe development arrives as Beijing doubles down on domestic energy security. A five-year development plan from the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration calls for intensified exploration to solidify independent supply. Reportedly, the target is 440 million tons of domestic oil and gas equivalent by 2030.Offshore production is already carrying much of that momentum. Data from the Ministry of Natural Resources shows China‘s offshore crude output climbed 3.5 percent year-on-year during the first nine months of 2026.Washington has long placed CNOOC on trade blacklists, including the Commerce Department’s Entity List and the Pentagon’s Section 1260H list, cutting off its access to advanced American oilfield services, specialized software, and deepwater drilling hardware. Reaching a nearly 6,000-meter depth without relying on Western oilfield giants like SLB, Baker Hughes, or Halliburton shows that Beijing’s push for technological self-reliance in energy infrastructure is paying off.U.S. energy majors like Chevron, Shell, and ExxonMobil routinely drill ultra-deep wells in the Gulf of Mexico. CNOOC’s project stands out because it targets volcanic rock in an active tectonic zone, whereas U.S. Gulf Coast drilling primarily focuses on sedimentary sandstone reservoirs.

title: 1,391 solar panels wrap 48-story building to turn it into a powerhouse
content: Developers in Australia have recently completed the installation of 1,391 solar panels into the facade, rooftop and crown of a Melbourne office tower, creating a building-integrated solar system capable of generating up to 375 kilowatts (kW) of power.The system has been installed in the 48-story building at 435 Bourke Street, Melbourne, and is expected to supply up to 20% of the building’s base electricity demand once fully operational by the end of the year.The project is billed as “one of the world’s first large-scale solar facades on a commercial office tower,” as Cbus Property, the building developer, claimed in a statement.Dual functions of ‘solar skin’The solar panels installed were described as “Solar skin” by the developers. The project was funded by the Australian government more than four years ago, which turned the tower’s walls into an electricity-producing surface instead of relying solely on rooftop panels.The building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) system covers more than 28,000 square feet (2,679 square meters) wrapped around the building, and expands the area available for solar generation in dense city environments where roof space is limited.Once operational, the system would meet the building’s energy demands, while lowering cooling demand and reducing electricity drawn from the grid.“The solar façade creates electricity but also acts as a sunshade that stops heat coming into the building,” Cbus Property Chief Executive Chris Kakoufas said. “This reduces operational costs for our tenant partners and emissions from grid electricity consumption, while creating a distinctive visual identity for the tower.”Not a simple mounting exerciseThe concept might sound simple; however, it was no easy feat.Delivering the system needed more than simply attaching solar panels to a skyscraper.Unlike the standard rooftop system, which is mounted onto a finished surface and can be removed without affecting the exterior, these BIPV systems replace conventional building materials such as facade cladding, glazing, shading, or roofing. These systems act both as a building element and an electricity generator.According to construction company Multiplex, the work required collaboration among different teams to meet construction quality and project schedule.“Integrating nearly 1,400 PV panels into the building envelope required not just technical smarts but also extensive coordination between the façade, structural and services teams to ensure no impact to quality or program,” said Ross Snowball, manager of Multiplex developers.Australian architectural firm Bates Smart was brought on board to design the façade so that the photovoltaic panels become part of the building’s appearance rather than an add-on.The final design included a textured exterior where the energy-generating panels function as both architectural elements and renewable energy infrastructure. The latest project is not the first Australian building to make power from its walls. An eight-story office building located at 550 Spencer Street in West Melbourne, equipped with 1,182 facade panels, was completed in November 2024.But the new building differs in scale.At 375 kilowatts peak, the Bourke Street system has more than double the reported capacity of the Spencer Street facade, on a 48-story tower rather than an eight-story building.​It provides a proof of concept for large-scale vertical solar installations, suggesting that the exterior walls of future skyscrapers could evolve from passive building shells into active power-generating systems.

title: Gas flow assisted flash evaporation deposits perovskite films at over 1 µm per minute without solvents
content:
Gas flow assisted flash evaporation deposits perovskite films at over 1 µm per minute without solvents
Researchers at the University of Valencia’s Institute of Molecular Science (ICMol) in Spain, together with
Oxford PV
, have developed a solvent-free vacuum technique for depositing perovskite films at rates above 1 µm per minute. The method, called gas flow assisted flash evaporation (Gas-FE), deposits films from a single pre-formulated powder, which the team says gets around the difficulty of controlling many separate sources in conventional co-evaporation.
In co-evaporation, each component needs its own source, and controlling the film composition gets harder as formulations become more complex, especially with trace additives. Deposition times can also run to hours. Earlier flash-evaporation approaches fed small amounts of powder into a heated crucible, which limited throughput. In Gas-FE, a ball-milled perovskite powder is fed by an auger screw into a nitrogen gas flow, forming an aerosol. The aerosol passes through a vaporizer held at 500 °C, and the vapor is carried through a heated showerhead onto a temperature-controlled substrate holder, at a roughing-pump vacuum of about 10 mbar. The team says this shortens turnaround between batches compared with high-vacuum deposition.
The researchers say the method transferred a mixture of components with widely different volatilities, including guanidinium iodide, amantadine hydrochloride, benzylphosphonic acid, lithium TFSI, formamidinium bromide, methylammonium iodide and lead iodide. They also report X-ray diffraction evidence of film formation from FA/Cs mixed-cation and mixed-halide powders.
For the main tests, the team used methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI₃) with 10 mol% methylammonium chloride and 8 mol% lithium TFSI. Films 100 to 1,100 nm thick were deposited by varying the powder injection time from 7 to 60 seconds, with a measured growth rate of about 18.6 nm/s (roughly 1.1 µm per minute). On a 10 × 10 cm² substrate area, the I:Pb ratio varied by less than 5% and the film thickness by 4%. Run-to-run variation was 6% to 8%.
The researchers integrated 250 nm films into a fully vacuum-deposited p-i-n solar cell (glass/FTO/MeO-2PACz/perovskite/C60/SnO₂/Cu). The best 0.05 cm² device reached a power conversion efficiency of 9.6%, with an open-circuit voltage of 0.91 V, a short-circuit current density of 16.8 mA/cm² and a fill factor of 63.3%. The team calls this a moderate, proof-of-concept result and says the spread in voltage and fill factor suggests that further improvement should focus on the interfaces and trap density.
The work was part of Spain’s PERTE Chip project, funded by NextGenerationEU.

content:
当地时间11月11日习近平主席特别代表、国家副主席韩正赴土耳其出席《联合国气候变化框架公约》第三十一次缔约方大会（COP31）安塔利亚领导人峰会并作国别发言时指出：
中国今年规划了2030年非化石能源发电量占比达到50%、电能占终端能源消费比重达到35%等目标，坚定不移推进碳达峰碳中和。中国也将为国际航空碳抵消和减排机制的公平有效实施作出贡献。
新华社土耳其安塔利亚11月11日电
在《联合国气候变化框架公约》第三十一次缔约方大会安塔利亚领导人峰会上的发言
（2026年11月11日，土耳其安塔利亚）
中华人民共和国副主席 韩正
当地时间11月8日至12日，习近平主席特别代表、国家副主席韩正赴土耳其出席《联合国气候变化框架公约》第三十一次缔约方大会（COP31）安塔利亚领导人峰会并作国别发言。这是当地时间11月11日，韩正在峰会作国别发言。
尊敬的埃尔多安总统，
女士们、先生们、朋友们：
很高兴作为中国国家主席习近平的特别代表，出席安塔利亚领导人峰会。习近平主席指出，应对气候变化是人类共同的事业。当前，全球气候变化不利影响加速显现。面对新形势，我愿提4点建议。
第一，锚定共同目标，强化集体行动。要遵循共同但有区别的责任原则，全面有效落实《联合国气候变化框架公约》及其《巴黎协定》，凝聚全球气候治理合力。发达国家应率先减排，兑现气候资金承诺。各方应全力落实国家自主贡献，力争做得更好。
第二，加快绿色转型，推进低碳发展。要促进优质绿色技术和产品自由流通，推动经济和产业结构转型升级。中国今年规划了2030年非化石能源发电量占比达到50%、电能占终端能源消费比重达到35%等目标，坚定不移推进碳达峰碳中和。
第三，防范气候灾害，提升气候韧性。要坚持减缓和适应并重，加强防灾减灾、监测预警、灾害救援等领域合作，提高气候适应能力。中国愿推动气象智能预警方案“妈祖”在更多国家落地应用，助力各国防范和应对气候风险。
第四，坚持开放普惠，深化国际合作。要加强对发展中国家的支持和帮助，共建清洁美丽世界。中国持续推进非洲光带等应对气候变化南南合作项目，将推出“全球南方气候行动领袖计划”能力建设项目。中国也将为国际航空碳抵消和减排机制的公平有效实施作出贡献。

content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has reaffirmed the UK’s commitment to net
zero by 2050 in a speech to the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
Speaking on the fourth day of the summit on 12 November, Burnham opened
“The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is upon us all now, devastating
lives and livelihoods everywhere."
He said two ongoing wars have pushed up gas and fuel prices, and that unpredictable
price swings meant the UK could no longer rely as heavily on fossil fuels.
“The common thread running through all of this, our dependence on fossil
fuels,” said Burnham.
The pledge comes as the government’s commitment to net zero has come under
scrutiny, following the approval of the Jackdaw gas field and continuing
questions over the Rosebank oil field.
Burnham backed the summit’s theme of electrification, saying it would
strengthen energy security, create jobs and lower household energy bills.
Adding that the approval of two Vanguard offshore wind projects the previous
day showed what that could deliver, with billions of pounds of investment,
power for millions of homes and thousands of jobs.
Burnham also announced the appointment of Dame Madeleine Alessandri as
the UK’s first special representative for climate security.
In addition, he confirmed support for the Amplify programme, which is expected
to unlock an estimated 5 billion in new private finance for clean energy
projects worldwide.

Eight North East England companies have been selected to take part in the

support, we can take the next step in developing Cyclonox and test its
potential to recover both energy and useful materials.

that supports the wind industry’s long-term sustainability.”

title: Where companies should place their AI bets
content: After several years of pushing organizationwide AI adoption, companies are now confronting the cost. As boardroom conversations shift to return on investment, business leaders are taking a harder look at which AI bets to fund and scale. To understand what questions executives should be asking ahead of AI investments, Meredith Mazzilli, The Information’s finance editor, spoke with three experts approaching AI from different perspectives. Karen Young, chair of the U.S. board of partners and U.S. sales leader, PwC Mimi Carsley, chief financial officer and treasurer, Jack Henry & Associates Heidi Rhodes, global director, enterprise GTM customer success and sales enablement, Meta Platforms Resetting Priorities At Meta Platforms, Mark Zuckerberg has taken an experimentation-first approach, making AI adoption a priority across the company. “He basically said, ‘This is going to be the year that everyone is going to adopt AI.’ We told our employees, ‘Figure out what works and go fail,’” recalled Heidi Rhodes. That freedom to experiment helped Meta identify which workflows benefited from AI and standardize around them. Initially, token consumption wasn’t a concern, a luxury Rhodes acknowledged not every organization can afford. “In 2023, it was: Any single problem that you have, rub some AI on it. Then we got our token bills,” she said. “Now organizations are saying, ‘Unless you can show me real ROI, we can end the conversation there.’” Other companies took a more cautious route. Jack Henry & Associates, which operates in the highly regulated financial services industry, started with governance, establishing guardrails for assessing and approving AI tools and determining what data employees could access, said CFO Mimi Carsley. At PwC, the challenge is less a shortage of ideas than deciding which ones are worth pursuing. Employees across PwC are embracing AI and exploring new ways to integrate it into their work. Karen Young said the deciding factor in funding ideas remains the client, much as it did before AI. “We think about the solutions our clients are looking for and how we can scale [our AI tools] for their benefit,” she said. Controlling Spend At Jack Henry, providing Microsoft Copilot licenses to all 7,300 associates could add $3 million in costs, said Carsley. The company therefore regularly reassesses who needs access. “If someone’s not using their license, we’ll go talk to them and coach them up. If they’re still not using it, we actually seize it back and redeploy it elsewhere in the organization,” she said. Young said PwC has also shifted to training employees to be more efficient with their usage. “We lead them to use the right tool for the right model for the right reason,” she said. Measuring What Matters One way organizations can prioritize AI spending is to look beyond efficiency gains to how those gains are put to use. By way of example, Young cited a client that transformed 14 finance processes, cutting forecasting and scenario planning from weeks to minutes. “The real question is: What are those employees in finance now doing to be more strategic with their time?” she asked. Carsley said companies also need to consider how they are using those time savings and whether they can redeploy investment elsewhere. “If someone’s gonna use AI to draft an email and you save five minutes, like, did you go get a cup of coffee or did you do something with the five minutes?” she said. “If you’re not redeploying that savings to another productivity or efficiency, did you really gain anything by the spend?” Rhodes, meanwhile, cautioned against treating efficiency gains as an excuse to reduce headcount. She cited a client whose sales team became 20% to 30% more productive after AI took over hours of research. “Do you make a reduction in humans? Or now that you have one of the world’s most efficient salespeople, do you go out and hire more?” she asked, adding that her vote is for the latter. Ultimately, though, AI prioritization comes down to a company’s unique advantage. “Ask yourself, what do you have an advantage in? Then apply AI to that as an accelerant,” advised Carsley. “Do the thing you do best as an organization, then turn it up 10% to 20%.”

title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
content:
More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
People with experimental brain implants are pushing for more recognition and respect.
Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”
The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).
Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”
Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.
He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it.
The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough.
Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”
In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition—an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.
The guidelines, published on Tuesday, lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”
As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.
The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.
Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data. Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.
The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.
“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”
The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago, he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.)
Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.
Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will—an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.
Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.
Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low. The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference.
“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”
