title: Abrupt End to Nvidia’s Jensen Drama Leaves Unanswered Questions
content: Jensen Huang’s long-running Nvidia drama ended on a cliffhanger with the news of the CEO’s resignation Thursday morning. We’re going to have to wait a while for the scriptwriters to figure out the next installment of this thriller. At the moment, we’ve got far more questions than answers: What happened between Sunday, when the board said it had confidence in Huang, and Wednesday night when Huang quit (as Nvidia revealed in a securities filing today)? What role did the Trump administration play in his departure? Astute watchers of the news media might have noticed that many of the numerous stories about the Wednesday night board meeting called to consider Huang’s future were at least partly written by Washington correspondents not normally reporting on Nvidia’s doings. Was the White House leaking stuff to pressure Huang to go? The answers will eventually come out, to be sure. But it’s likely to take a year or two for us to see the impact on Nvidia’s business of his departure, which is surely what investors most wonder about. However, the fact that shares of the AI chip giant bounced from its lows on Thursday is a sign that some investors think the sell-off of the past couple of days was overdone. The stock is still very cheap: At Nvidia’s closing price Thursday of around $166, the stock is trading at just 13.7 times forward earnings, compared with 38.9 for AMD, according to Koyfin data. While that gap seems huge, it’s not crazy given the uncertainty. We simply don’t have a clear idea of how much Nvidia will change without Jensen Huang. In our story this morning, for instance, we raised the question of whether a successor to Huang “will have the clout” to muscle key partners like chip manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. for capacity. In an interview on The Information’s TITV on Thursday, SemiAnalysis President Doug McLaughlin chimed in on a related point, about Huang’s influence on the road map for AI technology: “The whole ecosystem really rallied around Jensen…[he] was a singular person who kind of convinced everyone that this technology road map would come true and cajoled and bullied them, and obviously paid them quite a bit of money to really push advanced technical timelines.” Then there’s the question of whether his successor would be as willing to make such risky bets. McLaughlin noted that Huang locked up “a meaningful part of the supply chain” with aggressive commitments, ensuring that Nvidia had chips when others didn’t. He was able to gamble on those bets because he was the founder: Someone else might be more risk averse. We noted in our profile of interim CEO Colette Kress today that as finance chief, she sometimes pushed back on the deals he championed. See our other stories today on the Nvidia drama here , here and here . For the moment, Nvidia’s business should be fine. Multiple customers told us they expect Nvidia’s chips to keep selling out simply because they’re the best in the business. But it’s also likely some customers will feel more free to test alternatives than they would have in the past, when fear of offending Huang was a thing. This story will take a while to unfold. It could take the board six months to pick Huang’s permanent successor, for instance, and unless that person is an insider, they might not start right away. By the time Nvidia’s new management is installed, AI will have evolved several times over. HubSpot’s Shake-Up Within a couple of hours of Nvidia’s announcement that Jensen Huang was out, people were predicting his eventual return. Former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, for instance, posted on X that “3-4 years from now, NVDA will miss a quarter or two, and they will bring Jensen back to run the company.” The speculation isn’t crazy, given how often founders end up taking back the reins. The most famous example is Steve Jobs’ triumphant return to Apple in the late ’90s. We also saw it with Workday co-founder Aneel Bhusri in February , and we saw it today with HubSpot, when co-founder Brian Halligan took back the CEO job, five years after relinquishing it to Yamini Rangan, who had been chief customer officer under Halligan. Rangan didn’t do a bad job: As HubSpot acknowledged, she took the customer management software provider from $1.3 billion in revenue in 2021 to an expected $3.7 billion this year. But HubSpot’s stock has fallen 74% over the past five years, much of that occurring this year, thanks to investor worries about the threat posed to the software firm by AI. HubSpot may be particularly vulnerable to AI disruption, as its typical customers—small- and medium-size businesses—may be more likely to create their own sales software with AI tools. Indeed, we reported in July that several startups said they had ended contracts with HubSpot, as well as with Salesforce, in the previous six months in favor of AI-created apps. Halligan clearly feels he’s the one to tackle this challenge, just as Bhusri felt when he returned to Workday. Investors seemed to agree. HubSpot stock rose 6.4% on Thursday. In Other News • Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had affairs with at least two Nvidia employees while leading the company, Reuters reports . Separately, Huang has hired Paul, Weiss, a prominent white-collar law firm, according to The New York Times . • Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy at the heart of an Nvidia scandal , has been barred from Singapore after local authorities determined she had provided inaccurate information during an investigation they conducted into data center company Megaspeed. • Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla could unveil a merger as early as next month, Bloomberg reported Thursday. An announcement could still slip to early 2027. Directors and advisers are still negotiating how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive and how the merged company would be governed, the report said. title: How Much Is Anthropic Really Worth?
content: While investors digest the news of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang’s exit and its implications on the AI build-out , they are simultaneously mulling another nebulous question: How much is Anthropic worth? If everything goes according to plan, the market should give its answer when the company debuts on the Nasdaq exchange next week. Anthropic has set a tentative pricing range of between $1.25 trillion and $1.4 trillion, but several investors we spoke to expect it to price above that range. Pricing an initial public offering above the proposed range “is a signal of underlying demand momentum, which is very important to get people excited to participate,” said Samantha Lau, chief investment officer of small- and mid-cap growth equities at AllianceBernstein. The preliminary range is a bit lower than the $1.5 trillion or more expected by bankers over the last few months . Several investors suggested that the bottom of the company’s tentative range was directly influenced by the $1.25 trillion valuation at which OpenAI just fundraised . But as Anthropic’s business is bigger than OpenAI’s—$17 billion in the third quarter compared to OpenAI’s $10 billion —the Anthropic valuation appears too conservative. One way to consider the valuation is to assume Anthropic ends the year at roughly $100 billion in annualized revenue, a step up from the $81 billion it reported generating as of October—and then doubles that amount over the following two years. Applying an adjusted operating margin of 25%, a bit higher than the 19% it notched in the June quarter, to that higher revenue suggests Anthropic could earn roughly $50 billion in operating profit in 2028. That means its recently proposed valuation range implies a multiple of over 25 times 2028 EBIT. At a mid-20s EBIT multiple, Anthropic “would be kind of cheap relative to software multiples, a little bit richer relative to megacap tech, which I think directionally feels pretty reasonable,” said John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds who is considering buying shares in the Anthropic IPO. “I don’t think this is going to be a name where the question is about the multiple at these valuation ranges. I think it’s more about, can they sustain this pace of revenue growth at this scale?” Morningstar equity analyst Ahmed Khan estimates Anthropic is worth $1.7 trillion and projects that it will grow revenue at a 47% compounded annual growth rate over the next five years. Khan, in a November 11 report, said that even his bull case, which values the firm’s equity at $3.4 trillion, could be too conservative if Anthropic’s models reach the point where they can essentially train themselves to improve autonomously. Still, some investors note the valuation at which Anthropic debuts won’t reflect a financial analysis of the company’s near-term prospects. “The valuation question isn’t really driven by what is the ultimate free cash flow of the business, as much as it’s [driven by], can you grow to be the size of Google or Microsoft, and how fast can you get there?” said Willy Lee, principal at investment firm Neostellar, which runs an exchange-traded fund that holds shares in private companies such as OpenAI and Canva. Neostellar does not have a stake in Anthropic, but it invested in OpenAI over a year ago, according to Lee. One question is whether Nvidia’s executive shake-up could cause enough volatility in AI stocks to affect the Anthropic IPO. On one hand, any stumbles at Nvidia, which in some ways is propping up the AI sector with its prolific investments, might not bode well for Anthropic’s valuation. Gabelli Funds’ Belton points out that AI model makers including Anthropic “benefit from all the innovations that Nvidia consistently delivers. “To the extent that the innovation pipeline now slows down under new leadership at Nvidia, that inevitably has an impact on the pace of model development for the frontier models and for the pace of efficiency gains for serving these models,” Belton said. On the other hand, the best-positioned firm to weather the storm would be a company that is quite agnostic to what chip types come through, argued one investor at a large U.K.-based asset management firm that is attending Anthropic’s roadshow and considering participating in the IPO. “That would be Anthropic versus OpenAI or Google.” Asset managers almost always have to sell down something to buy into a new offering. The obvious candidate for funds looking for a slice of Anthropic would be to sell down AI infrastructure stocks, including semiconductor firms, the investor said. “Maybe some of the drawdown [in semiconductors] has been in anticipation of this.” Another question looming over Anthropic is whether it can sustain a breakneck pace of growth by pushing into new verticals now beyond AI coding assistants, which drove much of its growth this year. “If you’re comfortable with the broad strokes growth in AI, you then need to get comfortable with Anthropic not only growing that pie from the knowledge work side, but also whether they will be the one capturing that market share,” said Neostellar’s Lee. “I don’t know if they’ve necessarily proved that yet, which is why I think it’s a little bit more challenging for some folks to get comfortable on the valuation.” Ultimately, Anthropic’s valuation might hinge on market conditions outside its control that could hamper its growth trajectory or its ability to procure enough scarce computing power to train and run its models. “If I were a large-cap investor, I wouldn’t worry about profitability. I would only worry about financing, not just for Anthropic, but the whole entire ecosystem,” said AllianceBernstein’s Lau. title: Free Chinese AI Can Hack Companies While Frontier Developers Face Diminishing Returns
content: Chinese AI that anyone can download for free has become good enough to break into corporate networks, said Ariel Zeitlin, co-founder and chief technology officer of Tenzai, an Israeli startup that sells hacking software for testing corporate defenses, known as continuous penetration testing. At the same time, the most advanced AI that had an early lead in cybersecurity capabilities is getting harder and costlier to improve, said Micah Hill-Smith, CEO of AI benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis. That means Chinese models won’t be far behind and makes it unlikely that any one developer pulls far ahead of its rivals. The founders made the comments while speaking to The Information subscribers on Wednesday in a conference call after their companies appeared in our list of the 50 most promising startups of 2026 . Security startups featured more heavily in this year’s list than in past editions. “No one is restricting access to” the freely available Chinese open-weight models, Zeitlin said. “I think this is the real threat for…organizations.” He pointed to an open-source hacking tool, free to download, that has already been used to breach organizations. He didn’t name it, but security firms recently documented that attackers have used ARTEX , an AI hacking framework posted to GitHub in July. CrowdStrike said a China-linked group used it against more than 200 organizations in 11 days. “You don’t need to be a skilled hacker to do that,” Zeitlin said. Breaches Coming Zeitlin expects companies to endure a rough stretch of at least several months, if not years, with breaches disclosed daily, mostly because of software misconfigurations that AI makes easier to find. The biggest companies Tenzai works with, which employ thousands of security staff, are vulnerable too, he said. “Fixing is harder than finding,” he said. While Zeitlin has a financial incentive to make such statements, many security officials, executives and AI researchers developing models share such sentiments. Recent security lapses at AI developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic reflect startups’ looser habits, Zeitlin said, whereas big banks are better prepared. In the long run, he’s optimistic, saying that AI-written code will help companies avoid some bug types, such as injection flaws, but not the ones that arise when AI and applications interact. The free models worrying Zeitlin aren’t likely to fall far behind the most advanced ones, according to Hill-Smith. He said the race among AI developers has stayed “more competitive than expected.” OpenAI and Anthropic hold an edge of a few months at the frontier—“arguably Anthropic this week,” he said—with other U.S. and Chinese labs close behind. He said companies should keep investing in using open-weight models because “the ecosystem will be there,” meaning closed-source models won’t race ahead too far. Despite the lead held by closed-source models from the likes of Anthropic, open-weight models have continued to improve more than Hill-Smith expected because developers of such models get a lot of commercial opportunities from the notoriety their releases generate, he said. A Limit on Scaling Laws? Hill-Smith seemed to dismiss the idea of recursive self-improvement. He said that a so-called “fast takeoff” in which one developer’s models improve themselves so quickly that rivals can’t catch up was “pretty unlikely.” And in general, AI progress is bound to slow rather than speed up, in part because it will get harder for human experts to evaluate the work of new AI under development because it may already be on par with their level of expertise. In fact, he said, AI capability improvements per dollar of investment will keep shrinking, which is why companies like Anthropic and OpenAI need so much capital. And measuring their progress is going to get tricky if such companies are spending 10 times more to produce a model that’s twice as good. “The idea that it gets harder to make progress, I think, is true and will continue to be true,” he said. On the bright side, the cost to use AI for a given task at the same quality level is falling five to 10 times a year, he said, even as some of his firm’s tests of long-running agents now cost hundreds of dollars per task. title: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress Has Tried to Tame Nvidia’s Riskiest Bets
content: Nvidia’s appointment Thursday of its longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO will force the finance veteran to guide the business through a fraught storm of uncertainty created by the sudden resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang. Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013, when the business was a humble supplier of chips for gamers. And while she has played an important role in guiding the company’s ascendance to an all-important place in the AI economy, she wasn’t someone who set the agenda on the company’s major decisions, according to people familiar with Kress. Huang had run Nvidia with total control—and never established a clear succession plan. One person familiar with Kress said Huang tended to “steamroll” her whenever the two disagreed. Still, Kress is well known to the investment community. She is the only person other than Huang to regularly speak on Nvidia’s quarterly earnings calls. The next such call is Tuesday. Kress may take a more conservative approach than Huang did. As finance chief, she has sometimes pushed back on deals that Huang championed—including a proposed Nvidia backstop of $250 billion in credit support on behalf of OpenAI that would allow OpenAI to fill eight gigawatts of data center space with Nvidia’s newest-generation chips, according to people with knowledge of the deal discussions. In August, Nvidia ended up splitting the deal into two parts and has so far only guaranteed to backstop the first for around $100 billion in credit support. As data center delays and canceled cloud-computing deals have complicated the picture around the AI boom in recent months, Kress prioritized figuring out ways to ensure Nvidia’s financial risk wasn’t too concentrated in a handful of companies, those people said. Before Nvidia, Kress spent three years as chief financial officer of a Cisco division and more than a decade at Microsoft. On Wednesday evening, Huang stepped down from the company that he had led since its founding in 1993. His departure was swift—coming within days of Nvidia’s board announcing an inquiry into reports that he had an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. authorities believe was a Chinese spy. On Wednesday afternoon, news broke that he had also had an affair with a direct report, Kimberly Powell, a vice president responsible for Nvidia’s healthcare business. The relationship between Powell and Huang was widely discussed by employees, according to several former Nvidia employees. Huang on Sunday publicly apologized for being “unfaithful” to his wife, without naming Alice Huang, who was an executive at a major Nvidia customer under scrutiny for helping divert Nvidia chips to China. The board on Thursday morning said it would conduct a search for a permanent successor to Huang and would consider internal and external candidates. Current and former employees, plus other executives in the industry, have speculated that Nvidia’s Ian Buck could take the job. Buck, who is about 50, is currently the company’s vice president of high-performance computing and a key creator of CUDA, a software suite for programming Nvidia chips, and joined Nvidia in 2004. Investors greeted the news of Huang’s exit with displeasure on Thursday, sending the stock down nearly 7%. Nvidia shares have been hard hit by the scandal that has engulfed the company, falling more than 25% in the past two weeks. “I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in a message to Nvidia on staff on Thursday morning. “We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us.” She said she would host a company meeting next Wednesday, a day after Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report. In the same note, Harvey Jones, a founding Nvidia board member who will now become the company’s first-ever chair, described Kress as “key architect of Nvidia’s growth and capital strategy.” He also thanked Huang for his “profound” contributions to the company. Nvidia has poured more than $100 billion in investments, credit guarantees and other financial support into its customers and supply partners, assuming a unique role within the AI revolution as both the key supplier of the hardware needed to develop the technology and a major financial backer of its customers. The recent unease about the health of AI hadn’t seemed to bother Nvidia with Huang leading it. Nvidia had recently increased its investment in Anthropic to $10 billion, according to someone familiar with the discussions. Several AI investors and founders have expressed concern in the last few days that new investments and other financial support from Nvidia may be harder to come by. An executive at a cloud provider that buys Nvidia chips said the uncertainty around Huang is prompting the cloud firm to consider using other chips, such as those from Google or AMD. The firm previously considered such a move to diversify from Nvidia hardware but was afraid of offending Huang. Now, the executive said they are worried that Huang’s absence could negatively impact future generations of Nvidia chips, given how instrumental he was to the company. “We would be an idiot not to” consider other options, the person said. Preventing major customers from further diversifying to other chipmakers’ AI servers will be key among several challenges facing Kress and whoever takes over permanently. That said, multiple customers said they expect Nvidia’s chips will continue to sell out—at least in near term—and that the management shakeup won’t change the perception that the company’s AI server chips are the best in the business. Kress must also contend with Nvidia’s presence in D.C. Huang had grown close to President Donald Trump, advocating for America to change export bans that cut off Nvidia from selling chips to China. At the same time, Huang had made enemies in Washington over time , some of whom described his posture as “pugilistic” and said they felt bullied by him. Lawmakers from both parties have begun calling for tougher export controls on Nvidia’s chips and related products. Congress could pass such controls in the coming weeks as part of a collection of legislation called the National Defense Authorization Act. A House subcommittee has also asked Huang to testify behind closed doors at a hearing in Washington next week about his relationship with Alice Huang. At Nvidia, Kress not only sometimes disagreed with Huang but also came into conflict with his daughter, Madison, and son-in-law, Nico Caprez, both of whom have been rising stars there, according to two of those people. With Huang gone and Kress as interim CEO, the pair may see their sway within the company diminish.
